Chapter 2 · Origins · c. 800 a. C.–600 d. C.

Traditions of Asia, the Mediterranean and other regions

India and China developed sophisticated ideas about attention, the self, emotions and education, often left out of textbooks.

History of psychology textbooks usually start in Greece. It is an understandable habit, because academic psychology was born in Europe, but it leaves out traditions that reflected deeply on the mind and that are present again today, for example in mindfulness-based interventions.

What were people trying to understand?

In India, the Upanishads (from roughly the eighth century BCE) asked about the nature of the self and its relation to reality. Buddhism, from the fifth century BCE, focused on suffering: how it arises from craving and attachment, and how it can be eased by training the mind. In China, the great question for Confucian thinkers was practical: whether human nature is good or bad, and how education and custom shape character.

With what methods?

Systematic observation of one's own experience, sustained over years of practice. The Buddhist Abhidharma tradition produced detailed lists of mental states, their causes and their combinations, a kind of catalogue of experience. The Yoga Sutras, attributed to Patañjali, describe the mind as a stream of activity that can be stilled by training attention. In China, the method was dialogue, commentary on texts and reflection on social life.

Who took part?

Confucius (sixth to fifth century BCE) stressed learning and example as the drivers of character. Mencius held that we are all born with "sprouts" of compassion and shame that education must cultivate; Xunzi, by contrast, thought that without rules and effort human nature tends towards selfishness. Their debate echoes later arguments about nature and nurture. From the Sui dynasty (around 605 CE), China also created a system of imperial examinations to select officials on merit, which some historians see as one of the first large-scale uses of standardised tests.

What did it contribute?

  • Fine-grained descriptions of attention, craving and emotion, grounded in personal practice.
  • Mental training techniques that, adapted and secularised, are now studied with scientific methods.
  • An early debate on the role of education and environment in shaping character.
  • The idea of assessing abilities with tests common to all candidates.

What was revised later?

The Western adaptation of these traditions has sometimes been a simplification: the mindfulness taught in hospitals and companies leaves out much of its original ethical and philosophical framework. At the same time, research has shown that its effects are real but more modest than many adverts promise. More broadly, contemporary psychology increasingly recognises that its theories were built on samples from a handful of countries, and these traditions are a reminder that there are other ways of understanding the self, more relational and less individualistic.

There are many other traditions, in Africa, the Americas and the Islamic world, that deserve their own space. Some appear in chapters 4 and 22.

References

  1. Paranjpe, A. C. (1998). Self and Identity in Modern Psychology and Indian Thought. Nueva York: Plenum.
  2. Higgins, L. T. y Zheng, M. (2002). An introduction to Chinese psychology: its historical roots until the present day. The Journal of Psychology, 136(2), 225–239.
